claim: Hebb's idea of a cell assembly as the fundamental unit of neural information processing has dominated neuroscience for the past 60 years.
source: Hebb's idea of a cell assembly as the fundamental unit of neural information processing has dominated neuroscience like no other theoretical concept within the past 60 years.
evidence: This is a general statement about the historical influence of Hebb's concept in neuroscience, drawing from established scientific knowledge and consensus.

claim: Progress in cell assembly research is hampered by the lack of statistical tools that would enable extraction of assemblies with arbitrary constellations of time lags and at multiple temporal scales.
source: Yet progress in this area is hampered by the lack of statistical tools that would enable to extract assemblies with arbitrary constellations of time lags, and at multiple temporal scales, partly due to the severe computational burden.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' assessment of the current state of the field and inference about methodological limitations.

claim: The presented methodology detects assembly structure at many different time scales, levels of precision, and with arbitrary internal organization.
source: Here we present such a unifying methodological and conceptual framework which detects assembly structure at many different time scales, levels of precision, and with arbitrary internal organization.
evidence: This claim describes the capabilities of the methodology developed in the manuscript, supported by the data and analyses presented throughout the paper.

claim: There is no universal cortical coding scheme.
source: Applying this methodology to multiple single unit recordings from various cortical areas, we find that there is no universal cortical coding scheme, but that assembly structure and precision significantly depends on the brain area recorded and ongoing task demands.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from multiple cortical areas showing different assembly structures.

claim: Assembly structure and precision significantly depends on the brain area recorded and ongoing task demands.
source: Applying this methodology to multiple single unit recordings from various cortical areas, we find that there is no universal cortical coding scheme, but that assembly structure and precision significantly depends on the brain area recorded and ongoing task demands.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different brain areas and task conditions.

claim: The term 'cell assembly' lacks a stringent and universally accepted definition.
source: However, the term lacks a stringent and universally accepted definition, and has been used to denote anything from the precise zero-phase-lag spike synchronization in a defined subset of neurons (Abeles, 1991; Singer and Gray, 1995; Roelfsema et al., 1997; Diesmann et al., 1999; Harris et al., 2003) to temporally coherent changes in average firing rates on larger time scales (Goldman-Rakic, 1995; Durstewitz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to various studies that have used the term differently.

claim: Precise millisecond coordination of spike times for a 'volley' of activity has been reported in relation to specific perceptual or motor events.
source: Often the term is meant to imply precise millisecond coordination of spike times for a 'volley' of activity which repeats at regular or irregular intervals in relation to specific perceptual or motor events (Figure 1A, I; e.g. [Riehle et al., 1997; Roelfsema et al., 1997; Harris et al., 2003; Fries et al., 2007]).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Precise sequential patterns of spiking times have been reported in the hippocampal formation where they may correspond to sequential orders of places.
source: Precise sequential patterns of spiking times (i.e., with time lags ≠ 0) have been reported as well (Figure 1A, II), most commonly in the hippocampal formation where they may correspond to sequential orders of places (Skaggs and McNaughton, 1996; Buzsáki and Draguhn, 2004), in the visual cortex as a consequence of different activation levels (König et al., 1995), or as possibly generated through synfire-chain-like structures (Abeles, 1991; Diesmann et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Temporally ordered transitions among coherent firing rate patterns across sets of simultaneously recorded neurons have been described in different cognitive tasks and systems.
source: Such temporally ordered transitions among coherent firing rate patterns across sets of simultaneously recorded neurons have been described in different cognitive tasks and systems (Seidemann et al., 1996; Beggs and Plenz, 2003; Jones et al., 2007; Lapish et al., 2008; Durstewitz et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous studies.

claim: Sets of neurons jointly increasing their average rates for some period of time during persistent activity in a working memory task have been linked to the cell assembly idea.
source: At a still broader temporal scale, sets of neurons jointly increasing their average rates for some period of time (Figure 1A,V), as during persistent activity in a working memory task, have also been linked to the cell assembly idea (Durstewitz et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: There is an ongoing controversy about the degree of temporal precision and coordination present in neural activity and its relevance for neural coding.
source: There is indeed an ongoing, sometimes heated, controversy about the degree of temporal precision and coordination present in neural activity and its relevance for neural coding, partly based on empirical (Shadlen and Movshon, 1999; London et al., 2010), partly on statistical arguments (Mokeichev et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies representing different perspectives in the debate.

claim: The novel statistical approach treats the temporal scale, precision, and internal organization of coherent activity patterns as free parameters to be determined from the data.
source: Here we develop a novel statistical approach for multi-cell recordings that treats the temporal scale, precision, and internal organization of coherent activity patterns as free parameters, to be determined from the data, and is thus open to a large family of possible assembly definitions (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim describes a key feature of the methodology developed in the manuscript.

claim: The fast parametric test statistic automatically corrects for non-stationarity locally, avoiding computationally costly bootstrapping and sliding window analyses.
source: By deriving a fast parametric test statistic for pairwise dependencies that automatically corrects for non-stationarity locally, computationally costly bootstrapping and sliding window analyses are avoided, reducing the computational burden by factors of 100–1000 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim describes the computational efficiency of the method, with specific performance metrics provided.

claim: The computational burden is reduced by factors of 100–1000 compared to previous methods.
source: By deriving a fast parametric test statistic for pairwise dependencies that automatically corrects for non-stationarity locally, computationally costly bootstrapping and sliding window analyses are avoided, reducing the computational burden by factors of 100–1000 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim provides a quantitative comparison of computational efficiency.

claim: All five different types of assemblies were correctly identified with their associated temporal precision and lag distributions in simulated data.
source: The assembly-assignment matrix in Figure 1B demonstrates that all five different types of assemblies (and only these, no false detections) were correctly identified with their associated temporal precision and lag distributions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 1B from simulated data with known ground truth.

claim: No false detections occurred in the simulated data analysis.
source: The assembly-assignment matrix in Figure 1B demonstrates that all five different types of assemblies (and only these, no false detections) were correctly identified with their associated temporal precision and lag distributions.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 1B from simulated data.

claim: Assembly detection starts to significantly degrade only when the relative contribution to the spike series drops below approximately 4%.
source: Assembly detection starts to significantly degrade only when their relative contribution to the spike series drops below ~4% (Figure 2A), or when more than ~30% of all spike times were corrupted by spike sorting errors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic testing shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Assembly detection starts to significantly degrade when more than approximately 30% of all spike times were corrupted by spike sorting errors.
source: Assembly detection starts to significantly degrade only when their relative contribution to the spike series drops below ~4% (Figure 2A), or when more than ~30% of all spike times were corrupted by spike sorting errors (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by systematic testing shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The fraction of units falsely ascribed to any one assembly stayed uniformly low at about 0.5% across a whole range of sample sizes, spike assignment errors, and assembly structures tested.
source: More importantly, across a whole range of sample sizes, spike assignment errors, and assembly structures tested, the fraction of units falsely ascribed to any one assembly stayed uniformly low at about 0.5% (Figure 2C,D), indicating that our procedure is quite conservative and rarely returns false positives in the simulated scenarios.
evidence: This claim is supported by the results shown in Figure 2C and D.

claim: The procedure is quite conservative and rarely returns false positives in the simulated scenarios.
source: More importantly, across a whole range of sample sizes, spike assignment errors, and assembly structures tested, the fraction of units falsely ascribed to any one assembly stayed uniformly low at about 0.5% (Figure 2C,D), indicating that our procedure is quite conservative and rarely returns false positives in the simulated scenarios.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the low false positive rate shown in the data.

claim: Detected assemblies in ACC span a large range of temporal precisions, from approximately 10 ms to about 1.5 s.
source: Detected assemblies span a large range of temporal precisions, from ~10 ms to about 1.5 s, with a variety of lag distributions, and are composed of about 10% (ACC) to 16% (CA1, EC) of the recorded neurons.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of ACC data presented in Figure 3A.

claim: Detected assemblies are composed of about 10% (ACC) to 16% (CA1, EC) of the recorded neurons.
source: Detected assemblies span a large range of temporal precisions, from ~10 ms to about 1.5 s, with a variety of lag distributions, and are composed of about 10% (ACC) to 16% (CA1, EC) of the recorded neurons.
evidence: This claim provides quantitative data about the proportion of neurons involved in assemblies across different brain regions.

claim: Many of the experimentally recorded assemblies partially overlap (i.e., share units).
source: Note that different from the clear-cut hypothetical examples (Figure 1B) which were strictly disjoint by design, many of the experimentally recorded assemblies partially overlap (i.e., share units; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the experimental data analysis.

claim: Many of the unraveled assemblies were highly selective for specific task events.
source: Finally, many of the unraveled assemblies were highly selective for specific task events as illustrated in Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The joint (Δ,l)-distribution changes dramatically as the animals move from unstructured environmental exploration to a highly structured delayed alternation task.
source: Several features are noteworthy here: First, the joint (Δ,l)-distribution changes dramatically as the animals move from unstructured, completely self-paced, little demanding environmental exploration (Figure 4A, left column) to a highly structured, demanding delayed alternation task (Figure 4A, right column).
evidence: This claim is supported by the comparison shown in Figure 4A between different task conditions.

claim: During the delayed alternation task, a much larger number and richer repertoire of assembly structures turned out compared to environmental exploration.
source: During the latter, a much larger number and richer repertoire of assembly structures turned out, as also indicated by the 'marginal' distributions of significant unit pairs across time scales Δ in Figure 4B.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B comparing task conditions.

claim: Changes in ACC and CA1 assembly structures were mostly focused on the larger timescales when moving from exploration to delayed alternation.
source: However, secondly, while these changes in ACC and CA1 were mostly focused on the larger timescales, in EC they appeared to run across all timescales, yet were overall less dramatic than in CA1 (Figure 4A, bottom; Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: In EC, changes in assembly structures appeared to run across all timescales but were overall less dramatic than in CA1.
source: However, secondly, while these changes in ACC and CA1 were mostly focused on the larger timescales, in EC they appeared to run across all timescales, yet were overall less dramatic than in CA1 (Figure 4A, bottom; Figure 4B, bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: EC mainly harbors fine temporal structure with a precision of about 15–50 ms.
source: Third, assemblies remarkably differ among the three brain regions in the range of temporal scales they occupy: While EC mainly harbors fine temporal structure with a precision of about 15–50 ms, in ACC broad rate change patterns in the 120–700 ms range appear to dominate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: In ACC, broad rate change patterns in the 120–700 ms range appear to dominate.
source: Third, assemblies remarkably differ among the three brain regions in the range of temporal scales they occupy: While EC mainly harbors fine temporal structure with a precision of about 15–50 ms, in ACC broad rate change patterns in the 120–700 ms range appear to dominate (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: CA1 expresses a wide spectrum of temporal scales from about 30–1500 ms, of which the broader scales (>100 ms) only surface during delayed alternation.
source: CA1, in contrast, expresses both temporal scales, or in fact a wide spectrum from about 30–1500 ms, of which the broader scales (>100 ms) only surface during delayed alternation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the analysis of CA1 data across different task conditions.

claim: A much larger number of units engaged in any one assembly in CA1 (>90%) than in ACC (30–50%).
source: Overall, a much larger number of units engaged in any one assembly in CA1 (>90%) than in ACC (30–50%; Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim provides quantitative comparison of assembly participation across brain regions, supported by Figure 4B.

claim: The temporal composition and precision of assembly activity strongly depends on both the brain area and the behavioral setting.
source: These observations indicate that the temporal composition and precision of assembly activity strongly depends on both the brain area and the behavioral setting.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data comparing different brain areas and behavioral conditions.

claim: Some of the temporally more precise 30–50 ms assemblies in CA1 were found to code for specific place fields in the rat's environment.
source: On closer inspection, some of the temporally more precise 30–50 ms assemblies in CA1 were found to code for specific place fields ('place assemblies') in the rat's environment (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The temporally more precise assemblies in CA1 mainly consisted of synchronous (lag-0) spiking units.
source: These assemblies mainly consisted of synchronous (lag-0) spiking units (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The more broadly tuned assemblies in CA1 tended to code for temporally extended events which often appeared to have a specific behavioral meaning in the task context.
source: Meanwhile, the more broadly tuned assemblies in CA1 tended to code for temporally extended events which often appeared to have a specific behavioral meaning in the task context: For instance, these assemblies may become active during the reward event irrespective of its spatial location (Figure 5B), or for the whole correct choice path after a behavioral decision was made (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5B and 5D.

claim: The temporally broader assemblies in CA1 commonly followed a more sequential (lag≠0) layout.
source: These temporally broader assemblies commonly also followed a more sequential (lag≠0) layout (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: The single cells constituting CA1 assemblies did not necessarily share the same place preference with their 'parent' assembly.
source: Interestingly, the single cells constituting CA1 assemblies did not necessarily share the same place preference with their 'parent' assembly (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Broader assemblies in ACC were tuned to specific task phases and events (lever presses, delays, stimulus conditions) and reflected the task's sequential structure.
source: Similar as in CA1, broader assemblies in ACC were tuned to specific task phases and events (lever presses, delays, stimulus conditions) and reflected the task's sequential structure (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 3C and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The temporal structure and precision of the revealed assemblies were closely related to the computations performed by different brain areas.
source: Illustrating this methodology on multiple single-unit recordings from ACC, CA1, and EC, it appeared as if the temporal structure and precision of the revealed assemblies were closely related to the computations performed by these brain areas: While the CA1 region processes precise spatial (O'Keeffee and Nadel, 1978; Harris et al., 2003; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007) and temporal (Eichenbaum, 2014) environmental structure, the ACC is much less concerned with finely-granulated details of the spatial world (Hyman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the experimental data and supported by citations to previous work on the functions of these brain areas.

claim: The CA1 region processes precise spatial and temporal environmental structure.
source: While the CA1 region processes precise spatial (O'Keeffee and Nadel, 1978; Harris et al., 2003; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007) and temporal (Eichenbaum, 2014) environmental structure, the ACC is much less concerned with finely-granulated details of the spatial world (Hyman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on CA1 function.

claim: The ACC is much less concerned with finely-granulated details of the spatial world.
source: While the CA1 region processes precise spatial (O'Keeffee and Nadel, 1978; Harris et al., 2003; Diba and Buzsáki, 2007) and temporal (Eichenbaum, 2014) environmental structure, the ACC is much less concerned with finely-granulated details of the spatial world (Hyman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work on ACC function.

claim: Activity in ACC reflects behavioral organization, behavioral monitoring, overall context, and task structure, processes which typically unfold on much slower temporal scales.
source: Rather, activity in ACC reflects behavioral organization, behavioral monitoring, overall context, and task structure, processes which typically unfold on much slower temporal scales (Lapish et al., 2008; Hyman et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on ACC function.

claim: The hippocampal CA1 region has been reported to represent aspects of higher-order decision making, like paths to a defined goal state or choice outcomes.
source: Likewise, in addition to spatial coding, the hippocampal CA1 region has also been reported to represent aspects of higher-order decision making, like paths to a defined goal state or choice outcomes (Lisman and Redish, 2009; Buzsáki, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies on CA1 function.

claim: Sequential organization of assemblies at broader time scales was much more often observed in the delayed alternation task than in environmental exploration.
source: Consequently, sequential organization of assemblies at broader time scales was much more often observed in the latter than in the former task context.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the data comparing different task conditions.

claim: Most previous statistical procedures for detecting assemblies adhere to one or the other theoretical conceptualization of a cell assembly.
source: Numerous other statistical procedures for detecting assemblies or sequential patterns have been proposed previously (Grün et al., 2002a; Grün et al., 2002b; Pipa et al., 2008; Torre et al., 2016a), but most of these adhere to one or the other theoretical conceptualization of a cell assembly (cf. Figure 1A), or become computationally impractical for larger cell numbers or multiple lags (see Appendix for further discussion of both more recent and more 'traditional', cross-correlation-based, approaches).
evidence: This claim is based on citations to previous methods and comparison with the current approach.

claim: None of the previous methods combine all of the features presented in this work.
source: Also, none of these, to our knowledge, combines all of the features presented here.
evidence: This claim is based on the authors' knowledge of the literature and comparison with existing methods.

claim: There may be not just one type of cortical assembly code, but the temporal precision, scale, and sequential composition with which cortical neurons organize into coherent patterns strongly depends on the brain area and task context investigated.
source: Indeed, we observed that there may be not just one type of cortical assembly code, but that the temporal precision, scale, and sequential composition with which cortical neurons organize into coherent patterns strongly depends on the brain area and task context investigated.
evidence: This claim is a conclusion based on the experimental data from multiple brain areas and task conditions.

claim: The methods are not specific to the neuroscientific domain, but could be used more widely in other scientific areas to detect structure at multiple temporal scales in multivariate event count series.
source: We further note that our methods are not specific to the neuroscientific domain, but could be used more widely in other scientific areas to detect structure at multiple temporal scales in multivariate event count series.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the potential broader applicability of the methods.

claim: The agglomerative scheme is a fast heuristic proxy for evaluation of all possible unit and lag combinations.
source: The agglomerative scheme described above is a fast heuristic proxy, similar in spirit to the apriori algorithm in machine learning (Hastie et al., 2009; Picado-Muiño et al., 2013), for evaluation of all possible unit and lag combinations.
evidence: This claim describes the nature of the algorithm with reference to similar approaches in machine learning.

claim: In-vivo recordings from the rat anterior cingulate cortex were taken from two studies by Hyman et al.
source: The in-vivo recordings from the rat (Long-Evans) anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) were taken from two studies by Hyman et al. (Hyman et al., 2012; Hyman et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the source of experimental data used in the study.

claim: Multiple single unit recordings were performed with a set of 16 simultaneously implanted tetrodes in ACC, with an average of 35 and 30 isolated units per recording session for the environmental exploration and delayed alternation task, respectively.
source: In both studies, multiple single unit recordings were performed with a set of 16 simultaneously implanted tetrodes, with an average of 35 and 30 isolated (and artifact-free) units per recording session for the environmental exploration and delayed alternation task, respectively (with n=9 and n=11 sessions in total).
evidence: This provides specific details about the experimental recordings.

claim: Hippocampal and entorhinal cortex recordings on the exploration task were borrowed from Mizuseki et al. (2013).
source: Hippocampal and entorhinal cortex (EC) recordings on the exploration task, performed simultaneously within these two areas, were borrowed from (Mizuseki et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the source of experimental data used in the study.

claim: Recordings were collected from three Long-Evans rats implanted with multi-shank (32 or 64 sites) silicon probes lowered into the CA1 hippocampal pyramidal layer and into layers 3–5 of entorhinal cortex.
source: Recordings were collected from three Long-Evans rats implanted with multi-shank (32 or 64 sites) silicon probes lowered into the CA1 hippocampal pyramidal layer and into layers 3–5 of entorhinal cortex.
evidence: This provides specific details about the experimental recordings.
